'''Timothy Healey''' is an American [[applied mathematician]] working in the areas of [[Finite strain theory|nolinear elasticity]], [[nonlinear partial differential equations]], [[bifurcation theory]] and the [[calculus of variations]].<ref name="Birthday conference">{{cite web |last1=Healey |first1=Timothy |title=IUTAM Symposium: Tribute to Timothy Healey's 70th birthday |url=https://iutamstab2026.sciencesconf.org/ |website=Sciencesconf |publisher=IUTAM |access-date=6 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="Healey-Cornell">{{cite web |title=Timothy J. Healey |url=https://math.cornell.edu/timothy-j-healey |website=Cornell University Mathematics Department |publisher=Cornell University |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref> He is currently a [[professor]] in the Department of Mathematics, [[Cornell University]].<ref name="Healey-Cornell" />

Healey is known for his mathematical contributions to nonlinear elasticity particularly the use of [[group-theoretic]] methods in global bifurcation problems.<ref name="Birthday conference"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Antman |first1=Stuart |title=Nonlinear Problems of Elasticity |series=Applied Mathematical Sciences |date=2005 |volume=107 |publisher=Springer New York, NY |isbn=978-0-387-20880-0 |pages=142, 236, 318, 533 |edition=2nd |doi=10.1007/0-387-27649-1 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/0-387-27649-1 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="googlescholar">{{cite web |title=Healey's google scholar |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=e9KylCMAAAAJ&hl=en |website=Google Scholar |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Healey received his [[bachelor's degree]] in [[engineering]] from the [[University of Missouri]] in 1976 and worked as a [[structural engineer]] between 1978 and 1980.<ref>{{cite web |title=Short biography of Timothy Healey |url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~healey/Biographical%20Sketch.pdf |website=Cornell University Mathematics department |publisher=Cornell University |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref> He received his [[PhD]] in engineering from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] in 1985 under the guidance of Robert Muncaster in mathematics with mentoring from Donald Carlson and Arthur Robinson in [[mechanics]].<ref name="Math genealogy">{{cite web |title=Mathematics genealogy of Timothy Healey |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=28464 |website=Mathematics Genealogy |publisher=Mathematics Genealogy project |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref> He spent a [[postdoctoral]] year with [[Stuart Antman]] and P. Michael Fitzpatrick at the [[University of Maryland]] before joining the faculty at Cornell University, where he has held full-time positions in the Department of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics, Mechanical and Aerospace engineering and Mathematics.<ref name="UIUC biography">{{cite web |title=Timothy Healey biography |url=https://structures.cee.illinois.edu/files/2023/02/Professor-Timothy-J-Healey-.pdf |website=UIUC Structural engineering seminar series |publisher=University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign}}</ref> He has served as PhD advisor to 21 students, with 37 descendants.<ref name="Math genealogy"></ref>

== Research ==
Healey's research focuses on mathematical aspects of elasticity theory. Early in his career, he made fundamental contributions to the study of global [[bifurcation theory|bifurcation]] problems with [[symmetry in mathematics|symmetry]] using [[group theory|group-theoretic methods]], including work with H. Kielhöfer on the preservation of nodal properties in solutions of nonlinear [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic PDE]].  Along with many co-workers, his approach based on symmetry and global bifurcation/continuation has illuminated the behavior of a wide variety of physical systems, including rod structures, [[Lipid bilayer|lipid-bilayer vesicles]], [[Phase transition|phase transitions]], wrinkling in thin sheets, creasing in soft solids, and [[brittle fracture|brittle fracture]]. With H. Simpson, he developed a [[degree of a continuous mapping|topological degree]] similar to the [[Leray-Schauder degree]], yielding new [[existence|existence theorems]] in [[finite strain theory|nonlinear elasticity]].  Healey's work on [[transverse isotropy|transverse hemitropy and isotropy]] in [[François Cosserat|Cosserat]] rod theory is well known and provides a natural setting for studying the [[mechanics]] of [[ropes]], [[Wire rope|cables]] and biological filaments such as [[DNA]].  He has also established minimum-energy existence theorems for thin, nonlinearly elastic shells undergoing large membrane strains.<ref name="Birthday conference" /><ref name="googlescholar" /><ref>{{cite web |title=IUTAM Symposium on Global Bifurcation/Continuation in Nonlinear Elasticity: Modeling, Analysis and Computation |url=https://iutam.org/events/iutam-symposium-on-global-bifurcation-continuation-in-nonlinear-elasticity-modeling-analysis-and-computation |website=IUTAM |access-date=6 July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Antman |first1=Stuart |title=Nonlinear Problems of Elasticity |series=Applied Mathematical Sciences |date=2005 |volume=107 |publisher=Springer New York, NY |isbn=978-0-387-20880-0 |pages=309–318 |edition=2nd |doi=10.1007/0-387-27649-1 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/0-387-27649-1 |language=en}}</ref>
